sentences.text: 1. The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA Act), alleging that the accused persons has violated the provisions of the PFA Act and Rules.
The accused is stated to be the vendor-cum- proprietor of M/s. Manoj Sweets, from where the food article, that is, 'boondi ke laddoo' was lifted for sampling.

2. As per the complaint, on 03.08.2010, the food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI) P. M.
Kothekar and Field Assistant (FA) S. Maissey under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. V. P. Singh reached along with their staff at the premises of M/s. Manoj Sweets at In Re vs A-1) Manoj Kumar on 28 April, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/191839841/
1 shop No. T-39, Village Tehkhand, Okhla, New Delhi-110020, where the accused was found conducting the business of various food articles, which were lying stored for sale for human consumption.

entities.text: Manoj Sweets at In Re vs A-1) Manoj Kumar
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of boondi ke laddoo from the vendor, lying there in open tray bearing no label declaration, to which he agreed.
The sample was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.
Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the Notice as per Form-VI, panchnama, etc.
The price of sample was paid to the vendor.
Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.
Vide report dated 27.08.2010, the PA found the sample to be "misbranded" on the ground that the presence of synthetic colour was not declared as one of the ingredients.
Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by FI.
After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.

The complaint was then filed in the court on 09.03.2011 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) PFA Act and also Section 2 (ix) (d) and (e) of PFA Act, as punishable section 7/16(1A) of PFA Act.
3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused was summoned vide order dated 09.03.2011.

4. Notice of accusation under section 251 Cr.P.C was framed against the accused on 29.08.2012 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1)(a) PFA Act, being violation of section 2 (ix) (d) and (e) of PFA Act, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
It is pertinent to note that no notice was framed for violation of Section 2 (ia) (a) and (m) of PFA Act despite the complaint mentioning them, probably in view of the PA report.
5. At the trial, prosecution examined three witnesses in support of its case.

PW-1 FI, PW-2 SDM /
LHA and PW-3 FA were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings.

All these witnesses deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 03.08.2010 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 1500 grams of boondi ke laddoo,
dividing it in three parts, sealing, marking the samples, and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses.

They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex.PW-1/A,
Notice in Form VI Ex. PW-1/B, Panchnama Ex. PW-1/C, Report under Rule 9 (e) Ex. PW-1/D.
Receipt of PA Ex. PW-1/F and LHA receipt Ex. PW-1/G.
PA report Ex. PW-1/H was received and after obtaining consent of Director, PFA Ex.PW1/J, complaint Ex.PW1/K was filed.
These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence Counsel wherein they denied that the sampling method was not proper or that the accused had been falsely implicated.
6. Statement of the accused under section 313 CrPC was recorded on 17.09.2014 wherein he denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
Though he admitted the proceedings dated 03.08.2010, yet he claimed that the food article was not made by him and he had bought the same from some other person.
He denied the Public Analyst report.
He chose not to lead evidence in defence.

In Re vs A-1) Manoj Kumar on 28 April, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/191839841/
2 7.

It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused has not been able to rebut the findings of PA report dated 27.08.2010.
It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony.

8. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the present is not a case of misbranding as there is nothing to show that the article was coloured or polished to conceal the fact that it was damaged or it was made to appear of a greater value or that no any false claim had been made on its label.
9. I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and the Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused and have carefully perused the material available on record.
10. It is pertinent to note that notice against the accused was framed only for violation of Section 2(ix) (d) and (e) of PFA Act pertaining to the offence of misbranding.
He is not facing trial for the offence of adulteration as per Section 2(ia) of PFA Act.

He is not facing trial for the allegation that he had sold some article which was not of the nature, substance or quality demanded by the purchaser or was to his prejudice or was not of the nature, substance or quality which it purported or represented to be.
11. The report of PA nowhere shows that the colour tartrazine was not permitted or prohibited in any manner for use in the sample lifted from possession of the accused.

It is also to be noted that the PA has not mentioned / detected the percentage of synthetic colour Tartrazine present in the food article so as to ascertain if the same is beyond the permissible maximum limits or was injurious to health or was otherwise in violation of any other rule.

On the basis of this report, the prosecution /
complainant wishes the matter to be brought within the definition of "misbranding".
12.
At the same time, it is seen that the food article has no standard prescribed as such under the PFA Act or Rules.
It has been analyzed as "sweets" being a propriety food and not a standardized food product.
Since boondi ke laddoo is not a standardized for product, no fixed parameter has been prescribed under the Rules.

13. The only question is whether the matter would fall under sub Clauses (d) and (e) of Section 2(ix)
of the PFA Act.
14. As per record, the only evidence which is before the court is that the synthetic colour was found in the lifted sample which is otherwise permissible and not prohibited.

In such a position, there is no evidence that the food article was otherwise damaged or was of lower or lesser value than it was,
if the colour had not been there in the food product.
There is no evidence to show that the food article was so coloured to conceal any damage in the article or to make it appear better or of greater value than it was.
It cannot be said that addition of such colour has in any manner changed the nature or quality of the food product or has concealed any damage therein.
The report of PA nowhere shows any such damage or quality of the product which can be said to be a lesser or lower value than what has been declared by the accused in Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B.

In the said document, the In Re vs A-1) Manoj Kumar on 28 April, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/191839841/
3 accused has mentioned that the boondi ke laddoo were prepared by him using Vanaspati, Sugar and Refind soyabean oil.
There is no evidence to show that there was any defect in the said ingredients which was sought to be concealed by the accused by the use of permitted synthetic colour Tartrazine.
Therefore, clause (d) of Section 2(ix) of PFA Act would not come into picture.

15. Similarly, there is nothing to show that any false claim had been made by the accused with respect to food product so as to bring the matter within the purview of clause (e) of Section 2 (ix) of PFA Act.
Apparently, there is no label on the food product which was lying in open tray.
The provisions of labeling under Rule 32 of PFA Rules are applicable only to packaged / prepackaged food products and not to the products lying in open or sold loose.
Even otherwise, there is nothing to show that any false claim had been made by the accused even in Form -VI Ex.PW-1/B.

Though mentioning of presence of food colour in the food product is not there in the said form, but there is nothing to show that any false claim as such had been made with respect to absence of any such synthetic colour at the time of sale of the food article.

In view of this position, this court is of the view that the case does not fall within the purview of "misbranding" as alleged by the complainant /
prosecution.
16. The accused is entitled to be given benefit of doubts, and is therefore acquitted of the charges.

However, his bail bond shall remain in force for the next six months in terms of Section 437-A Cr.P.C.
17.
File be consigned to record room.
